sections.skill: Evaluate whether an AI feature works across languages, accents and disabilities

questions.prompt: Why check access across groups?

choices.text: A feature is useful only if it works for those who need it
Because features always work equally well for every user

questions.correct_answer: A feature is useful only if it works for those who need it
questions.intro: An AI feature is only useful if it works for the people who need it. Check ACCESS across LANGUAGES (does it handle Spanish, Tagalog or Navajo as well as English?), ACCENTS and dialects (does speech recognition understand everyone?), and DISABILITIES (can blind users operate it with a screen reader? does it handle speech differences? are captions accurate?). Use MEASURED evidence, such as error rates per group from testing with real users, rather than assumptions. The 2020 speech study is one example of measuring gaps between groups.

sections.skill: Compare AI access with a building's entrances

questions.prompt: Who does a staircase-only entrance shut out?

choices.text: Nobody, since every visitor can always climb stairs easily without any help at all

questions.correct_answer: Wheelchair users and others
questions.intro: A building with only a staircase entrance works fine for many visitors, but not for wheelchair users, parents with strollers or delivery workers with carts. Adding a ramp and an elevator lets more people in. An AI feature that only works with spoken English is like the staircase: it works for some and shuts out others. Offering alternatives, like typing and other languages, is like adding the ramp.

questions.prompt: Adding a ramp is like what in AI?

choices.text: Removing the typing option, so that every user must speak to the feature instead

questions.prompt: Why are access problems often invisible to the building team?

choices.text: The team may not share the users' needs
Because access problems do not exist for any feature that is built by a careful team

questions.correct_answer: The team may not share the users' needs
questions.intro: Access problems are often invisible to the team that built a tool. A voice-only feature excludes people who cannot speak or hear well; a feature that works only in English excludes many users. Offer alternatives, such as typing as well as speaking, and test with the people who will use the feature, including disabled users, paying them for their time where possible. Report results honestly, including groups where the feature works poorly.
